intro: Arithmetic is the craft of working with numbers: how they are written, how the four operations combine them, and how fractions, decimals and percentages describe parts of a whole. These lessons build from place value through ratios, with enough practice that each idea stands on its own. Use pencil and paper; calculators are optional after you can do the steps by hand.
name: Arithmetic
title: Arithmetic foundations

lessons.title: Place value

sections.p: In the base-ten system, each digit’s value depends on its place. Moving one place left multiplies by 10; moving one place right divides by 10.
In 3,482 the 3 is thousands (3 × 1000), the 4 is hundreds, the 8 is tens and the 2 is ones. Expanding: 3000 + 400 + 80 + 2.
10¹ = 10, 10² = 100, 10³ = 1000. A digit in the 10ⁿ place means that digit times 10ⁿ.
To compare two numbers of the same length, compare digits from the left. The first place that differs decides which is larger. Extra leading zeros do not change the value: 0042 = 42.

lessons.summary: Ones, tens, hundreds and how a digit’s place changes its value.

practice.why: The 7 sits in the hundreds place, so it contributes 7 × 100 = 700.
practice.q: In 5,703, what is the value of the digit 7?

practice.why: Each step left is ×10 in base ten.

lessons.title: Addition and subtraction

sections.p: Addition combines quantities. Subtraction finds how much is left or how far apart two numbers are. Addition and subtraction undo each other: if a + b = c, then c − b = a.
Align place values. Add from the ones column. When a column sums to 10 or more, write down the ones digit and carry 1 (or more) to the next place.
If the top digit is smaller, borrow 1 from the next left place (that place loses 1; this place gains 10).

lessons.title: Multiplication

sections.p: Multiplication a × b means b groups of a (or a groups of b). It is repeated addition: 4 × 3 = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
Commutative: a × b = b × a. Associative: (a × b) × c = a × (b × c). Distributive over addition: a × (b + c) = a×b + a×c. Multiplying by 0 gives 0; by 1 leaves the number unchanged.
Multiply by each digit of the second factor, shifting left one place for tens, two for hundreds, then add the partial products.
×10 appends a zero to a whole number; ×100 appends two zeros. 45 × 100 = 4500.

lessons.summary: Repeated addition, the times table and multi-digit products.

practice.why: ×10 shifts one place left / appends a zero.
Any number times zero is zero.
Order of factors does not change the product.
practice.q: Which property says a × b = b × a?

lessons.title: Division

sections.p: Division asks how many equal groups, or how large each group is. a ÷ b (or a/b) is the number of times b fits into a. If it does not fit evenly, there is a remainder.
For whole numbers, a = b × q + r with 0 ≤ r < b. Example: 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2, because 5×3 + 2 = 17.
Work from the left: how many times does the divisor fit into the leading digits? Write that digit of the quotient, subtract, bring down the next digit, repeat.
If a ÷ b = q with no remainder, then b × q = a. Division by zero is undefined: there is no number q with 0 × q = a when a ≠ 0, and every q works when a = 0.

lessons.summary: Sharing into equal groups, quotients and remainders.

practice.why: Division by zero is not defined.
Remainder is strictly smaller than the divisor.

lessons.title: Fractions

sections.p: A fraction a/b (b ≠ 0) means a equal parts when the whole is split into b equal parts. The top number is the numerator; the bottom is the denominator.
Multiply or divide numerator and denominator by the same nonzero number: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6. Simplest form cancels common factors.
With the same denominator, larger numerator is larger. Otherwise find a common denominator, or cross-multiply: a/b ? c/d compares a×d with b×c (when b,d > 0).
Add/subtract only after a common denominator: a/c + b/c = (a+b)/c. Multiply: (a/b)×(c/d) = (ac)/(bd). Divide by multiplying by the reciprocal: (a/b)÷(c/d) = (a/b)×(d/c).

lessons.summary: Parts of a whole: equivalent fractions, comparing, add and multiply.

practice.why: Multiply top and bottom of 1/2 by 3.

lessons.title: Decimals

sections.p: Digits after the decimal point are tenths, hundredths, thousandths, … So 0.35 = 3/10 + 5/100 = 35/100 = 7/20.
In 12.407 the 4 is tenths, 0 is hundredths, 7 is thousandths. Trailing zeros after the point do not change value: 1.50 = 1.5, but they can show precision.
Line up the decimal points and work column by column, same as whole numbers.
Multiply as whole numbers, then place the decimal so the product has as many digits after the point as the factors have combined. 1.2 × 0.3: 12×3=36, two decimal places → 0.36.
You may move the decimal in divisor and dividend the same number of places to make the divisor a whole number, then divide.

lessons.summary: Tenths and hundredths, linking decimals to fractions and place value.

practice.why: One digit after the point means tenths.

lessons.title: Percentages

sections.p: Percent means “per hundred”. 25% = 25/100 = 0.25. Percents are a convenient language for discounts, tax and test scores.
Percent → decimal: divide by 100 (move the point two places left). Decimal → percent: multiply by 100. Fraction → percent: divide, then ×100, or scale denominator to 100 when easy.

sections.h: Finding a percentage of a number

sections.p: Increase of p% means multiply by (1 + p/100). Decrease of p% means multiply by (1 − p/100). A 20% off sale on $50 costs 0.8×50 = $40.

lessons.summary: Per hundred: converting among percents, fractions and decimals.

practice.why: ×100 moves the point two places right.

practice.q: If a test score is 18 out of 20, the percent is:

sections.p: When an expression mixes operations, evaluate in a fixed order so everyone gets the same answer. A common mnemonic is PEMDAS / BODMAS: parentheses (brackets) first, then exponents (orders), then multiplication and division left to right, then addition and subtraction left to right.
A fraction bar groups the numerator and the denominator. Compute top and bottom before dividing.
Without a shared order, 3 + 4 × 2 could mean 14 or 11. The rule is a convention, but it is the convention used in algebra and calculators (scientific mode).

practice.why: Exponents before multiply and add: 8×4=32, then 5+32.

lessons.title: Integers

sections.p: Integers are …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, … Negatives sit to the left of zero on the number line. Temperature below zero, debt and elevation below sea level all use negatives.
|a| is the distance from a to 0, always ≥ 0. |−5| = 5 and |5| = 5.
Same signs: add the absolute values and keep the sign. Different signs: subtract the smaller absolute value from the larger and keep the sign of the larger.
a − b = a + (−b). Subtracting a negative is adding: 4 − (−2) = 4 + 2 = 6.
Same signs → positive product/quotient. Different signs → negative. (−2)×(−3)=6; (−2)×3=−6.

lessons.summary: Negative numbers, absolute value and signed arithmetic.

practice.why: Absolute value is distance from zero.
Different signs; 5−3=2 with the sign of 5.
Further left on the number line.
Same signs: add absolutes, keep negative.

lessons.title: Ratios and rates

sections.p: A ratio a:b (or a/b) compares two quantities of the same kind. A rate compares different kinds (km per hour, price per kg). A unit rate has a denominator of 1.
Scale both parts by the same factor: 2:3 = 4:6 = 6:9. In fraction form this is the same as equivalent fractions.
A proportion says two ratios are equal: a/b = c/d. Cross-multiply: a×d = b×c. Solve for a missing part with that rule.
If 3 apples cost $1.50, the unit price is $1.50 ÷ 3 = $0.50 per apple. Unit rates make comparisons easy.

lessons.summary: Comparing quantities by division; proportions and unit rates.
